title: "Unequal Visibility of AI Futures for Education in Vietnamese News"
author:
  - name: "Vu Nguyen Quang Duy"
    affiliations:
      - name: "Hiroshima University"
        department: "Graduate School of Humanities and Social Sciences"
    email: "duyvnq@gmail.com"

abstract: |
  News coverage presents multiple futures for artificial intelligence (AI) in education, but gives them unequal visibility. This study examines 828 articles from 20 Vietnamese news outlets using the Sociotechnical Imaginaries in Public Communication framework. Five future roles organise the analysis, with evaluations, speakers, reasons, and proposed actions linked within attributed accounts and compared at article level. AI as a Learning Partner appeared in 60.5% of articles and AI Literacy as an Educational Imperative in 53.0%, ahead of Educational Judgment (37.7%), National Development (19.6%), and Educational Management (10.3%). Public/central outlets gave greater attention to AI Literacy and National Development than commercial/general outlets, alongside more frequent public-authority voices and proposals for curriculum and resources. Learning Partner and Educational Judgment had similar overall visibility across the groups, but their evaluations differed: negative assessments of Educational Judgment appeared in 49.7% of commercial/general articles containing that role, compared with 28.8% of public/central articles. Across the corpus, desirable futures appeared in 96.0% of articles and undesirable futures in 33.1%. Close reading shows that warnings could support both restrictions and proposals for responsible AI use. The central pattern is an uneven distribution of attention within a shared set of educational futures: institutional preparation receives greater emphasis in public/central coverage, while commercial/general coverage gives more space to problems of educational judgment. These differences show which futures gain public visibility and institutional justification, and where their terms remain contested.

```{r}
#| label: setup-methods

library(tidyverse)
library(kableExtra)

# Locate project data when rendering from manuscript/ or the project root.
project_root <- if (file.exists("results/article_coding.csv")) "." else ".."
articles <- read_csv(file.path(project_root, "results/article_coding.csv"),
                     na = "", show_col_types = FALSE)
outlets <- read_csv(file.path(project_root, "data/outlet_classification.csv"),
                    show_col_types = FALSE)
main <- articles |> filter(main_sample == 1)

stopifnot(
  !anyDuplicated(articles$article_id),
  !anyDuplicated(outlets$outlet_domain),
  !anyNA(articles$main_sample),
  all(articles$main_sample %in% c(0, 1)),
  all(articles$outlet_domain %in% outlets$outlet_domain),
  all(main$eligibility == "clear_future"),
  all(articles$outlet_group ==
      outlets$outlet_type[
        match(articles$outlet_domain, outlets$outlet_domain)
      ])
)
```



```{r}
#| label: setup-analysis
#| include: false

book <- jsonlite::fromJSON(file.path(project_root,
  "data/sipc_future_coding/codebook.json"), simplifyVector = FALSE)
field_names <- c(future_role = "Future role", certainty = "Certainty",
  desirability = "Desirability", rationale = "Rationale",
  technology_object = "Technology characteristics", education_context = "Technology context",
  timespan = "Timespan", space = "Space", speaker = "Speaker",
  affected_entities = "Affected entities", action = "Action recommendation",
  responsibility = "Action responsibility")
labels <- imap_dfr(book$fields, function(entries, field) {
  map_dfr(entries, function(e) tibble(field = field, code = e$code,
                                     category = e$label))
})
roles <- labels |> filter(field == "future_role") |>
  mutate(short = c("LP", "EJ", "EM", "AL", "ND"))
role_ids <- roles$code
records <- lapply(readLines(file.path(project_root,
  "data/sipc_future_coding/coded_corpus.jsonl"), warn = FALSE),
  jsonlite::fromJSON, simplifyVector = FALSE)
records <- Filter(function(x) x$ID %in% main$article_id, records)
stopifnot(length(records) == nrow(main),
          setequal(vapply(records, `[[`, character(1), "ID"), main$article_id),
          all(paste0("future_role__", role_ids) %in% names(main)))
accounts <- map_dfr(records, function(record) {
  map_dfr(seq_along(record$accounts), function(i) {
    a <- record$accounts[[i]]
    tibble(article_id = record$ID, account = i,
           position = a$position, codes = list(a$codes))
  })
}) |> left_join(main |> select(article_id, outlet_group), by = "article_id")
# Keep role–field links within one attributed account, then deduplicate by article.
linked <- pmap_dfr(accounts, function(article_id, account, position, codes, outlet_group) {
  rr <- intersect(unlist(codes$future_role), role_ids)
  if (!length(rr)) return(tibble())
  imap_dfr(codes[names(codes) != "future_role"], function(values, field) {
    crossing(role = rr, code = unlist(values)) |>
      mutate(article_id, account, position, outlet_group, field)
  })
})
role_articles <- linked |> distinct(article_id, outlet_group, role)
role_pairs <- linked |> filter(code != "MISSING") |>
  distinct(article_id, outlet_group, role, field, code)
role_n <- function(role, group = NULL) {
  d <- role_articles |> filter(.data$role == .env$role)
  if (!is.null(group)) d <- d |> filter(outlet_group == group)
  nrow(d)
}
role_count <- function(role, code, group = NULL) {
  d <- role_pairs |> filter(.data$role == .env$role, .data$code == .env$code)
  if (!is.null(group)) d <- d |> filter(outlet_group == group)
  n_distinct(d$article_id)
}
# Missing means no substantive code in this field in any account bearing this role.
role_missing <- function(role, field, group = NULL) {
  d <- role_pairs |> filter(.data$role == .env$role, .data$field == .env$field)
  if (!is.null(group)) d <- d |> filter(outlet_group == group)
  role_n(role, group) - n_distinct(d$article_id)
}
article_count <- function(code, data = main) {
  stopifnot(code %in% names(data))
  sum(data[[code]] == 1, na.rm = TRUE)
}
pct <- function(code, data = main) sprintf("%.1f", 100 * article_count(code, data) / nrow(data))
rp <- function(role, code, group = NULL) {
  sprintf("%.1f", 100 * role_count(role, code, group) / role_n(role, group))
}
cell <- function(n, denominator) sprintf("%d (%.1f)", n, 100 * n / denominator)
for (r in role_ids) {
  stopifnot(setequal(role_articles$article_id[role_articles$role == r],
    main$article_id[which(main[[paste0("future_role__", r)]] == 1)]))
}
# Existing primary designation is retained; it is not recoded for this manuscript.
primary <- main
for (record in records) {
  selected <- Filter(function(a) identical(a$position, "primary"), record$accounts)
  stopifnot(length(selected) == 1L)
  i <- match(record$ID, primary$article_id)
  for (field in names(selected[[1]]$codes)) {
    values <- setdiff(unlist(selected[[1]]$codes[[field]]), "MISSING")
    cols <- grep(paste0("^", field, "__"), names(primary), value = TRUE)
    for (column in cols) {
      suffix <- sub(paste0("^", field, "__"), "", column)
      primary[[column]][i] <- if (suffix == "missing") as.integer(!length(values)) else
        if (length(values)) as.integer(suffix %in% values) else NA_integer_
    }
  }
}
publication_groups <- c("public/central", "commercial/general")
role_prevalence <- map_dfr(role_ids, function(r) {
  vals <- vapply(c("All", publication_groups), function(g) {
    d <- if (g == "All") main else filter(main, outlet_group == g)
    cell(article_count(paste0("future_role__", r), d), nrow(d))
  }, character(1))
  tibble(Role = roles$category[match(r, role_ids)],
         All = vals[[1]], Public = vals[[2]], Commercial = vals[[3]])
})
profile_rows <- labels |> filter(field != "future_role") |>
  bind_rows(tibble(field = names(field_names)[-1], code = "MISSING",
                   category = "No assigned substantive code")) |>
  arrange(match(field, names(field_names)), code == "MISSING",
          match(code, labels$code))
profile_table <- function(group = NULL) {
  rows <- profile_rows
  for (i in seq_len(nrow(roles))) {
    r <- role_ids[[i]]
    rows[[roles$short[[i]]]] <- map2_chr(rows$field, rows$code, function(f, c) {
      n <- if (c == "MISSING") role_missing(r, f, group) else role_count(r, c, group)
      cell(n, role_n(r, group))
    })
  }
  groups <- rows |> count(field, name = "rows") |>
    arrange(match(field, names(field_names)))
  rows |> select(category, all_of(roles$short)) |>
    kbl(format = "latex", booktabs = TRUE, longtable = TRUE, linesep = "",
      col.names = c("Category", paste0(roles$short, " (n=",
        vapply(role_ids, role_n, integer(1), group = group), ")")), align = "lrrrrr") |>
    kable_styling(latex_options = "repeat_header", font_size = 8,
                  repeat_header_text = "(continued)") |>
    column_spec(1, width = "5.8cm") |>
    column_spec(2:6, width = "1.55cm") |>
    pack_rows(index = setNames(groups$rows, field_names[groups$field]),
              indent = FALSE, latex_gap_space = "0.4em")
}
```
# Introduction

AI is expected to personalise learning, change assessment, simplify educational administration, and prepare people for new forms of work. These futures can reinforce one another, but they make different demands on education. A system that helps students finish tasks faster may also reduce the effort through which they learn. A tool introduced to protect academic integrity may place greater authority in an automated judgment. The question is therefore not simply whether AI is welcomed, but which educational futures are advanced through it and which receive sustained attention.

Imagined futures matter because they help organise present choices. They give reasons to invest, revise curricula, develop infrastructure, and assign responsibilities. Sociotechnical imaginaries connect such technological expectations to visions of social order and collective life [@jasanoff2009; @jasanoff2015]. Their plurality does not imply equal influence: some acquire institutional backing and resources, while others remain proposals, qualifications, or objections. Studies of national AI strategies show how governments connect technological development to public purposes and make particular directions actionable [@bareis2022]. Education is central to this process, both as a field to be transformed and as a means of preparing people for the anticipated future [@rahm2023].

Policy documents make formally endorsed directions visible. News offers another view of the same process, bringing official programmes into contact with commercial promises, expert judgments, and accounts of educational experience. It is a space in which futures are publicly articulated, repeated, justified, and questioned [@brause2024; @brause2025]. Examining this space reveals both the range of futures in circulation and the unequal attention given to them. Connecting an envisioned role for AI to its speakers, evaluations, reasons, and recommended actions makes that inequality more informative than a general measure of optimism.

Vietnam provides a setting in which educational and national ambitions are closely connected. Its 2021 national AI strategy and 2022 education digital-transformation programme position education as both a site of technological application and a source of future capabilities [@vietnam2021; @vietnam2022]. Research on five major Vietnamese state newspapers during 2016–2022 found optimistic AI narratives, national-development aspirations, substantial industry participation, and limited discussion of ethical issues [@nguyen2026]. An education-specific analysis can show how these broad aspirations take shape in proposals for learning, assessment, institutional management, and AI-related preparation.

Differences within Vietnamese news are equally relevant. Party-state oversight and commercial pressures coexist, while outlets differ in institutional affiliation, publishing orientation, and audience [@nguyenthu2019; @luong2022]. Comparing public/central and commercial/general outlets therefore allows attention to variation within a shared media environment. The issue is which futures and voices receive greater attention in each group, including where similar aspirations coexist with different evaluations.

This study examines `r nrow(main)` articles from `r length(unique(main$outlet_domain))` outlets using the Sociotechnical Imaginaries in Public Communication (SIPC) framework. Five future roles organise the analysis; the remaining fields establish how each role is evaluated, justified, and connected to action. Two questions guide the study:

> RQ1. Which futures for AI and education are articulated in Vietnamese news, how are they constructed, and which are most prevalent?

> RQ2. How do the visibility and construction of these futures differ between public/central and commercial/general outlets?

The central finding is an uneven distribution of attention within a shared set of educational futures. Learning support and preparation for an AI-oriented world lead the coverage. Public/central outlets give greater attention to institutional preparation and collective development, while commercial/general outlets more frequently include negative assessments of educational judgment. The contribution lies in these differences in emphasis and construction, rather than in the novelty of the five roles themselves.

# Literature Review

## Educational purposes in sociotechnical imaginaries of AI

Sociotechnical imaginaries are collectively held visions of desirable futures in which technological development is connected to ideas about social life and social order [@jasanoff2009; @jasanoff2015]. Their significance lies in how they guide present choices: which problems deserve attention, which technologies merit investment, and which institutions should act. National AI strategies, for example, connect technological capabilities to ambitions for economic development and international standing, helping justify programmes and allocate responsibilities [@bareis2022]. Studying imaginaries therefore involves examining the social commitments carried by technological promises, including whose expectations gain institutional support [@hendriks2025].

Education occupies two positions in these futures. It is expected to benefit from new technologies and to prepare people for the society those technologies are expected to produce. @rahm2023 shows how expectations of technological change become demands for education, skills, and particular forms of citizenship. These demands depend on how the problem is defined. If the problem is a shortage of technical skills, the proposed response may be curriculum reform. If it is students’ dependence on automated assistance, the response may involve limits on use or changes to assessment. @rahmskageby2023 argue that educational AI proposals contain such problem definitions, which shape what becomes a reasonable or necessary intervention.

Research identifies several purposes behind these proposals. @nemorin2023 connect educational AI discourse to economic development, geopolitical competition, and market expansion. Other work examines promises of wider access and changes to teachers’ work, showing how expected benefits depend on resources, institutional support, and pedagogical relationships [@bulathwela2021; @hrastinski2019]. Critiques of efficiency and performance also ask what these priorities leave out. An approach that values faster completion or measurable achievement may give less attention to care, curiosity, critical judgment, or the experience of learning itself [@mamlok2025; @wieczorek2026]. These studies make educational purpose central to the analysis: the significance of an AI application depends on what it is expected to improve and how improvement is judged.

The relationship among these purposes remains an empirical question. Saving teachers’ time may be justified as a way to provide more individual attention, linking efficiency to care. Developing AI skills may serve both professional preparation and national economic ambitions. Yet the same purposes can also support different approaches. Protecting independent thought might justify teaching students to question AI outputs or restricting their access to them. Research on educational imaginaries shows that competing understandings of improvement can coexist within the same policy setting [@linderoth2024]. Analysis must therefore examine how purposes are connected to practices and responsibilities, rather than treating personalisation, efficiency, or skills development as self-explanatory visions.

Warnings also help define desired futures. Concerns about dependence, inequality, or the loss of human capabilities can establish conditions under which a technology becomes acceptable [@cave2019]. A call to limit AI use may seek to protect an educational goal that advocates of adoption also value. Positive and negative evaluations consequently need to be read in relation to their targets: what is being welcomed or feared, whose interests are at stake, and what response is proposed.

## Public communication and the analysis of educational futures

News media make technological expectations publicly available through decisions about what to cover, whom to quote, and how to describe anticipated change. Their coverage brings official programmes into contact with commercial claims, expert judgments, and accounts of everyday experience [@brause2025]. Studies of AI reporting show that these expectations vary across national settings, where technological benefits and risks become connected to different political priorities and institutional arrangements [@brause2024; @wang2025]. Variation also occurs within a polity: government, business, academic, and civic actors may advance different expectations about AI [@richter2025].

Access to this public discussion is uneven. Some actors appear as authorities entitled to explain technological change, while others appear mainly as people who will experience its consequences. Research on educational AI reporting identifies imbalances in actor representation that can favour institutional priorities over educators’ and learners’ concerns [@huang2025]. This distinction matters when asking whose future is being described. An article may repeatedly discuss benefits for students without including students’ judgments about those benefits. Likewise, teachers may be assigned responsibility for successful implementation without being given comparable scope to define its purposes. Attention to voice must therefore distinguish speaking about a future, being affected by it, and being expected to deliver it.

The Sociotechnical Imaginaries in Public Communication (SIPC) framework provides a way to examine these distinctions systematically. It treats publicly communicated futures as visions of desirable or undesirable technological change that can orient action towards their realisation or prevention [@brause2025]. Its six dimensions cover vision, desirability, futures, technological object, speaker, and implications. These are operationalised through twelve fields, shown in @tbl-sipc.

| Theoretical dimension | Analytical field | Question guiding analysis |
|---|---|---|
| Vision | Future role | What educational or social change is expected, sought, or feared? |
| Vision | Certainty | How firmly is that outcome predicted? |
| Desirability | Desirability level | How does the speaker evaluate the anticipated change? |
| Desirability | Affected entities | Who is expected to experience its consequences? |
| Desirability | Rationale | What reasons or values support the evaluation? |
| Futures | Timespan | When is the change expected to occur? |
| Futures | Space | Where is it expected to apply? |
| Technological object | Technology characteristics | What form of AI is involved? |
| Technological object | Technology context | In what educational setting is it expected to operate? |
| Speaker | Speaker | Who articulates the future, and in what capacity? |
| Implications | Action recommendation | What action or restraint is proposed? |
| Implications | Action responsibility | Who is expected to act or be accountable? |

: SIPC dimensions and the questions used to examine educational AI futures. Adapted from @brause2025. {#tbl-sipc}

The framework’s value lies in connecting these fields. A forecast of improved learning means something different when improvement refers to higher test scores, stronger independent judgment, or wider participation. Its meaning also depends on whether the proposed change is justified by a provider, a teacher, or a learner, and whether it requires new products, different teaching practices, or restrictions on use. Counting each element separately can show what receives attention. Reconstructing their connections shows the educational future being proposed.

@brause2024 organised their healthcare analysis around themes in AI’s envisioned role, then examined the other analytical elements in relation to each role. This study follows that logic across a larger educational corpus. Future roles provide the organising categories; their evaluations, speakers, reasons, and implications establish how they are constructed. A role can contain both welcomed and feared developments, and similar evaluations can support different practices. Reading these connections preserves variation within a role without treating every favourable or critical statement as a separate imaginary.

News evidence also sets the scope of this interpretation. Public articulation is one part of the collective and institutional life of imaginaries; it does not establish that audiences accept a vision or that institutions have adopted it [@jasanoff2015; @hendriks2025]. Repetition requires similar care. Several outlets may circulate the same announcement or quotation, increasing its visibility without adding independently expressed support. The analysis therefore treats recurrence as evidence of circulation and examines attribution and source context before interpreting agreement.

## Educational AI futures in Vietnam’s media context

Vietnam’s national AI strategy and education digital-transformation programme assign education a role in technological development. They support AI applications in education while calling for the skills and specialist expertise needed to strengthen national capabilities [@vietnam2021; @vietnam2022]. Education consequently appears both as a public service to be improved and as a means of pursuing wider development goals. These policy commitments provide a reference point against which news accounts can promote applications, describe institutional initiatives, or question whether particular uses serve educational needs.

Such reporting takes place within a media environment shaped by party-state oversight and commercial pressures. Institutional supervision and editorial guidance influence permissible coverage, while advertising, sponsorship, and competition for audiences affect publishing priorities [@nguyenthu2019; @luong2022]. These pressures coexist within outlets. Their institutional affiliations and publishing orientations nevertheless differ, providing a basis for examining variation in the actors and educational expectations they make visible.

@nguyen2026 found prevailing optimism and national-development aspirations in AI reporting by five major Vietnamese state newspapers during 2016–2022. They also identified substantial industry participation and limited attention to ethical issues. These findings suggest that developmental ambitions and commercial participation can occupy the same news space. An education-specific analysis can examine how that relationship is expressed through proposals for curricula, teaching, assessment, and institutional investment. It can also ask whether concerns about learning and professional judgment qualify the terms on which technological expansion is supported.

The comparison between public/central and commercial/general outlets addresses this variation. The labels describe institutional profiles and publishing orientations within the same political environment. Public/central outlets may give greater attention to official programmes and collective responsibilities, while commercial/general outlets may foreground applications, products, and educational experiences. These are possibilities to investigate, not positions assigned to the groups in advance. Official and commercial actors can promote similar initiatives, and criticism of AI use can appeal to the same educational or national goals invoked by its advocates.

The analytical question is therefore how each group connects purposes to people and proposed action. Differences in the frequency of learner voices, for example, matter partly because learners may introduce concerns absent from institutional announcements. Similar support for professional preparation may conceal disagreement about whether competence requires greater AI use or protection from dependence. Examining these relationships allows the study to assess both variation across outlet groups and the educational commitments that cross their boundaries.

# Methodology

## Research design and corpus construction

This study combined qualitative analysis of educational AI futures with descriptive comparisons across Vietnamese news outlets. The Sociotechnical Imaginaries in Public Communication framework supplied six dimensions and twelve analytical fields. Categories within these fields were developed from the collected texts. Articles were the units of sampling and descriptive comparison. Within each article, attributed statements about educational futures were coded to retain connections among expected outcomes, evaluations, speakers, and proposed actions.

Articles were retrieved through Google News RSS searches targeting 21 Vietnamese outlet domains and publications dated between 2017 and 2026. Queries combined Vietnamese terms for AI and education with named technologies and terms concerning assessment and academic integrity. Search vocabulary was adapted across three periods: 2017–2021, 2022–2023, and 2024–2026. **[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM: collection dates, the final publication-date cutoff, and the basis for selecting the 21 domains.]** Duplicate search hits were consolidated, titles screened for relevance, and publisher URLs resolved before article texts and metadata were extracted. When initial extraction returned incomplete content, alternative retrieval procedures were used to recover the article. The collection procedure sought to retrieve all available matches across the specified queries and periods. Google News RSS nevertheless limits results per query, so this effort cannot establish exhaustive coverage of indexed or published news. The current project directory retains the retrieved corpus and validation/export scripts, but not the original crawling and scraping scripts.

Source adequacy and eligibility were assessed separately. Source checks identified missing article bodies, unrelated webpage content, and unavailable audiovisual transcripts. Where possible, incomplete texts were replaced with fuller versions of the same publication. Eligibility required an anticipated or normatively desired educational change involving AI. Reports of current applications qualified when they connected those applications to an expected educational outcome or direction. A reference to AI adoption, technical performance, university affiliation, or a course title alone was insufficient.

The working corpus contained `r format(nrow(articles) + 17L, big.mark = ",", trim = TRUE)` records. Verification of article–extraction linkages identified 15 records without recoverable original identifiers and two duplicate extraction records associated with one original identifier. These 17 records were excluded as storage and linkage errors. Of the `r format(nrow(articles), big.mark = ",", trim = TRUE)` retained articles, `r sum(articles$eligibility == "clear_future")` contained clear educational futures, `r sum(articles$eligibility == "borderline_future")` were borderline, `r sum(articles$eligibility == "no_educational_future")` did not contain a supported educational future, and `r sum(articles$eligibility == "unresolved_source")` remained unresolved because the source material was inadequate. The main analytical sample comprised `r nrow(main)` clear-future articles, excluding `r sum(articles$eligibility == "clear_future") - nrow(main)` for which the producing publisher was uncertain.

`r length(unique(articles$outlet_domain))` of the targeted outlets contributed retained articles; *khoahocphattrien.vn* contributed none. Outlets were classified as public/central or commercial/general according to institutional affiliation and publishing orientation (@tbl-outlet-classification). Assignments were established independently of article tone and coding outcomes. The classification is deliberately approximate: institutional affiliation and commercial publishing practices can overlap within either group. These operational groups do not distinguish state ownership from private ownership or directly measure political and commercial influence. The main sample contained `r sum(main$outlet_group == "public/central")` public/central articles and `r sum(main$outlet_group == "commercial/general")` commercial/general articles.

Each retained article was linked to its original identifier, publication metadata, URL, source text, and text hash. Eligibility decisions and publisher-uncertainty flags were retained in the project dataset. Source materials, extraction and coding protocols, the final codebook, and validation and export scripts are retained in the project dataset. **[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM: repository or supplementary-materials link before submission.]**

## Extraction and coding

AI-assisted open extraction first organised relevant material into the twelve SIPC fields, preserving attribution, qualifications, and conflicting evaluations. Attributed accounts then served as coding units within articles. An account could span several sentences and was distinguished by its speaker position, proposed arrangement, or evaluation target. This retained the connection between a future claim and the reasons or actions attached to it.

The final five future-role categories were informed by the researcher’s exploratory coding of 100 articles and subsequent review of the existing extraction and coding records. The revision applied these categories to the corpus while retaining eligibility decisions, account boundaries, and coding in the other eleven fields. Existing accounts and open extractions provided the starting point; source passages were revisited when a role or its target required clarification. A warning or implementation condition could inherit the role of a clearly identified programme, tool, or continuing attributed argument, but not another speaker’s evaluation or intention. Accounts without a supported role remained unassigned.

The five categories are defined in @tbl-role-definitions. They describe the educational relationship or collective purpose being imagined, rather than its desirability. AI as a Learning Partner therefore includes accounts of impaired learning through dependence as well as accounts of useful assistance. Similarly, AI as a Force Reshaping Educational Judgment includes threats to authentic achievement and proposals to protect it. Multiple roles were permitted when an account explicitly supported more than one.

| Future role | Analytical boundary |
|---|---|
| AI as a Learning Partner | Changes to learning, learner development, and relations among learners, teachers, and AI. |
| AI as a Force Reshaping Educational Judgment | Changes to assessment, academic integrity, authenticity, and recognition of achievement or competence. |
| AI as an Educational Management Tool | Changes to operations, administration, institutional services, monitoring, and resource allocation. |
| AI Literacy as an Educational Imperative | Preparing people to understand, develop, critically use, and live or work with AI. |
| AI as a Driver of National Development | AI-related education or university research serving an explicitly stated collective, sectoral, or national development purpose. |

: Five future roles and their boundaries. Full inclusion and exclusion rules are retained in the codebook. {#tbl-role-definitions}

Desirability was coded separately for the relevant speaker and target. Positive and negative statements from different speakers, or about different arrangements, remained separate. Explicitly mixed evaluation required one speaker to weigh desirable and undesirable effects of the same arrangement. Unsupported fields remained missing. Consequently, positive and negative evaluations could coexist in an article without an explicitly mixed account, and a positively evaluated safeguard could express a critical response to AI use.

Source-linked evidence and automated checks supported traceability. Checks verified identifiers, permissible codes, record structure, and the location of evidence in retained source texts. These procedures did not constitute independent intercoder validation. The current analysis reports no verified agreement coefficient for the revised five-role coding. **[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM: model identifiers, run dates, configurations, and the documented division of researcher and AI work. Any independent reliability result must specify its sample, coders, fields, and applicability to this codebook before inclusion.]**

## Descriptive comparison and interpretation

The article-level CSV defined the analytical sample and all main descriptive comparisons. Each code counted once per article, regardless of the number of accounts carrying it. Overall prevalence used `r nrow(main)` articles as its denominator; outlet comparisons used `r sum(main$outlet_group == "public/central")` public/central and `r sum(main$outlet_group == "commercial/general")` commercial/general articles. Missing fields remained in the denominator. Multiple codes were permitted, so percentages need not sum to 100%.

Profiles within each future role used the attributed-account records to preserve links that the article-level CSV alone cannot establish. A role and another field had to occur within the same account before the pair was counted. Each article then contributed at most once to each role–code pair. Percentages used the number of articles containing the role, within the full sample or the specified outlet group. Missing meant that no account bearing that role supplied a substantive code in the field. This approach measures the presence of a linked feature within a role; it does not imply that all features in a profile were expressed together by one speaker.

Desirability, rationale, speaker, action, and responsibility receive emphasis because they show how a future is valued, justified, and made actionable. The complete profiles retain certainty, affected entities, technology, educational context, time, and space (Appendix A). No account was excluded from a role’s profile because it lacked a rationale or action. The analysis does not rank multi-field combinations, which would favour accounts explicitly supplying every selected field and could make brief warnings less visible.

Counts and percentages describe this retrieved corpus. Article presence measures how widely a future appears, not its textual prominence or the strength of endorsement. An existing designation of the primary account provides a separate descriptive check on prominence. Selected outlet comparisons were also repeated after omitting each outlet in turn; these existing sensitivity checks are reported in Appendix B. Neither procedure changes the main article-level unit.

Close reading examined how the coded relationships were expressed in full source passages. Cases were selected to clarify recurring proposals, contrasting evaluations, and exceptions to the group-level pattern. Quotations reproduce complete sentences and paragraphs from retained source texts in English translation. Attribution identifies the speaker’s role or institutional capacity rather than their personal name; quoted journalistic narration is identified as such. Article identifiers link quotations to their publications. Qualitative contrasts describe practices interpreted from these passages, not additional coded groups with separately measured prevalence.

# Results

## Learning support and AI preparation lead an uneven field of futures

AI as a Learning Partner and AI Literacy as an Educational Imperative dominated the coverage by article prevalence. They appeared in `r pct("future_role__FR_LEARNING_PARTNER")`% and `r pct("future_role__FR_AI_LITERACY")`% of the sample, respectively (@tbl-role-prevalence). The first concerns what AI might do for learning; the second concerns what people must learn in response to AI. Educational Judgment formed a substantial third strand, while National Development and Educational Management appeared less frequently. The coverage thus placed educational practice and preparation ahead of institutional administration as explicit objects of future change.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-role-prevalence
#| tbl-cap: "Future-role prevalence by outlet group, articles n (%)."
role_prevalence |>
  kbl(format = "latex", booktabs = TRUE, longtable = TRUE, linesep = "",
      col.names = c("Future role", "All (828)", "Public/central (424)", "Commercial/general (404)"),
      align = "lrrr") |>
  kable_styling(latex_options = "repeat_header", font_size = 9) |>
  column_spec(1, width = "6.4cm") |> column_spec(2:4, width = "2.4cm")
```

*Note.* Each role is counted once per article; roles can coexist. `r article_count("future_role__missing")` articles in the main sample had no assigned future role and remain in the denominator.

The profiles distinguish these futures by their educational focus (Appendix A). Learning Partner accounts connected AI to learning quality in `r rp("FR_LEARNING_PARTNER", "RATION_PEDAGOGY")`% of the 501 articles containing that role and to changes in teaching, learning, or assessment practice in `r rp("FR_LEARNING_PARTNER", "ACT_PRACTICE")`%. Educators, researchers, and specialists were its most frequent speaking category. A VnExpress contribution by a representative of VioEdu, an FPT educational platform, described a shift in teachers’ work:

> In fact, AI will not be able to replace teachers’ roles entirely. However, their work in the classroom will change. With AI applied in teaching, teachers take on an observational role and concentrate on communication and emotions—areas in which machines cannot yet replace humans.
>
> — VioEdu/FPT representative, *VnExpress* ([VNE19_004](https://vnexpress.net/tri-tue-nhan-tao-thay-doi-nen-giao-duc-tuong-lai-3971688.html))

In the same article, AI-supported administration was expected to free teachers’ time for professional work. Learning Partner and Educational Management were therefore complementary: administrative relief was justified through the educational relationships it would enable. Across the 85 articles containing Educational Management, operational feasibility and efficiency was its most frequent rationale (`r rp("FR_EDUCATIONAL_MANAGEMENT", "RATION_CAPACITY")`%), while providing resources or implementation capacity was its most frequent action (`r rp("FR_EDUCATIONAL_MANAGEMENT", "ACT_RESOURCES")`%). Its smaller presence did not make it a competing alternative to learning; it often concerned the conditions under which educational work could be organised.

AI Literacy moved the object of change from AI-assisted learning to people’s capacity to understand and use AI. Its accounts linked changes in practice with curriculum reform and resources, and assigned responsibility to educational organisations in `r rp("FR_AI_LITERACY", "RESP_ED_ORG")`% of the 439 articles containing the role. National Development extended preparation towards an explicit collective goal. Within its 162 articles, resource provision (`r rp("FR_NATIONAL_DEVELOPMENT", "ACT_RESOURCES")`%) and curriculum change (`r rp("FR_NATIONAL_DEVELOPMENT", "ACT_CURRICULUM")`%) were the leading actions, while public authorities and educational leadership were the leading speaking categories. The difference was the end being pursued: individual or professional capability in AI Literacy, and collective technological or workforce capacity in National Development.

Educational Judgment focused on what would count as credible achievement when AI could produce assessed work or participate in judging it. Rights, reliability and academic integrity was its leading rationale (`r rp("FR_EDUCATIONAL_JUDGMENT", "RATION_RIGHTS_INTEGRITY")`% of 312 articles). Changing educational practice and setting rules were both common responses. This role therefore connected technological change to the authority to recognise learning, rather than merely to the efficiency of producing work.

## Public/central coverage gives greater weight to institutional preparation

The outlet difference was strongest around preparation and collective development. AI Literacy appeared in `r pct("future_role__FR_AI_LITERACY", filter(main, outlet_group == "public/central"))`% of public/central articles and `r pct("future_role__FR_AI_LITERACY", filter(main, outlet_group == "commercial/general"))`% of commercial/general articles; National Development appeared in `r pct("future_role__FR_NATIONAL_DEVELOPMENT", filter(main, outlet_group == "public/central"))`% and `r pct("future_role__FR_NATIONAL_DEVELOPMENT", filter(main, outlet_group == "commercial/general"))`%, respectively. Educational Management was also more frequent in public/central coverage. Learning Partner and Educational Judgment, by contrast, had similar prevalence across the two groups. The comparison points to different emphases within a shared set of futures.

Public/central coverage also more frequently included public authorities, policy-based rationales, and proposals for curriculum and resources (@tbl-outlet-features). Commercial/general coverage included learner voices more often: `r pct("speaker__SPK_LEARNER", filter(main, outlet_group == "commercial/general"))`%, compared with `r pct("speaker__SPK_LEARNER", filter(main, outlet_group == "public/central"))`%. These distributions locate the group difference in both what futures receive attention and whose accounts enter the discussion.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-outlet-features
#| tbl-cap: "Selected speaking positions, rationales, and actions by outlet group, articles n (%)."
selected <- c("SPK_PUBLIC", "SPK_ED_LEADERSHIP", "SPK_ACADEMIC_EXPERT", "SPK_LEARNER",
              "RATION_POLICY", "ACT_CURRICULUM", "ACT_RESOURCES", "ACT_COORDINATE",
              "ACT_EVALUATE", "RESP_PUBLIC", "RESP_ED_ORG")
rows <- labels |> filter(code %in% selected) |> arrange(match(code, selected))
for (g in publication_groups) {
  d <- filter(main, outlet_group == g)
  rows[[g]] <- map2_chr(rows$field, rows$code,
    function(f, c) cell(article_count(paste0(f, "__", c), d), nrow(d)))
}
groups <- rows |> count(field, name = "rows") |> arrange(match(field, .env$rows$field))
rows |> select(category, all_of(publication_groups)) |>
  kbl(format = "latex", booktabs = TRUE, longtable = TRUE, linesep = "",
      col.names = c("Category", "Public/central (424)", "Commercial/general (404)"), align = "lrr") |>
  kable_styling(latex_options = "repeat_header", font_size = 9) |>
  column_spec(1, width = "8cm") |> column_spec(2:3, width = "2.8cm") |>
  pack_rows(index = setNames(groups$rows, field_names[groups$field]), indent = FALSE)
```

*Note.* Denominators are all articles in each outlet group. These are separate article-level distributions; the role profiles in Appendix A require linkage within the same account.

The institutional direction was explicit in reporting on the education ministry’s draft AI strategy. The report connected widespread AI use to a nationally developed educational ecosystem:

> The strategy sets the overall objective of applying AI comprehensively and systematically across the education sector, towards building a modern, effective, and sustainable digital education system. Looking towards 2035, AI will become a common tool for every learner, teacher, and education manager, while an AI ecosystem developed by Vietnamese enterprises will be used consistently in general education.
>
> — Report of the Ministry of Education and Training’s draft strategy, *Giáo dục Việt Nam* ([GDN25_005](https://giaoduc.net.vn/bo-giao-duc-va-dao-tao-xay-dung-chien-luoc-ung-dung-ai-trong-giao-duc-post250172.gd))

The article specified curriculum integration, teacher preparation, infrastructure upgrades, institutional rules, and partnerships with technology companies. These proposals gave the envisioned future a timetable and a set of responsible organisations. Its account of safeguards was part of that direction: privacy, responsible use, and testing before wider deployment were presented as requirements for implementation.

Collective development was also advanced through educational and commercial initiatives. In coverage of a school AI and robotics competition, an FPT University admissions director explained its purpose:

> In the context of the Fourth Industrial Revolution, artificial intelligence (AI) and robotics are increasingly establishing their key role in social development. Early exposure to and application of these technologies, especially among school pupils, is an important factor in guiding and developing talent and preparing a high-quality workforce for the country.
>
> — Admissions director, FPT University, *Giáo dục Việt Nam* ([GDN25_006](https://giaoduc.net.vn/chinh-thuc-khoi-dong-cuoc-thi-ai-robotics-danh-cho-hoc-sinh-thpt-toan-quoc-post250193.gd))

Here a competition connected pupils’ activities to national workforce formation. Together with the draft strategy, the account shows how government and educational providers could advance compatible expectations through different programmes. The National Development role did not belong exclusively to government speakers, just as a public/central outlet did not publish only official voices.

## Critical evaluations concentrate on learning and educational judgment

Desirable futures appeared in `r pct("desirability__DES_POSITIVE")`% of articles, compared with `r pct("desirability__DES_NEGATIVE")`% for undesirable futures. The imbalance was substantial, but criticism was concentrated rather than uniformly scarce. Negative evaluations occurred in `r rp("FR_LEARNING_PARTNER", "DES_NEGATIVE")`% of articles containing Learning Partner and `r rp("FR_EDUCATIONAL_JUDGMENT", "DES_NEGATIVE")`% of those containing Educational Judgment, compared with much smaller shares for AI Literacy, Educational Management, and National Development (@tbl-role-evaluations). The roles receiving the strongest affirmative evaluations were therefore not the same as those carrying the most visible disputes about use.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-role-evaluations
#| tbl-cap: "Evaluations linked to each future role, percentage of articles containing that role."
evals <- map_dfr(role_ids, function(r) tibble(
  Role = roles$category[match(r, role_ids)],
  Desirable = rp(r, "DES_POSITIVE"), Undesirable = rp(r, "DES_NEGATIVE"),
  Mixed = rp(r, "DES_MIXED"),
  Public = rp(r, "DES_NEGATIVE", "public/central"),
  Commercial = rp(r, "DES_NEGATIVE", "commercial/general")))
evals |>
  kbl(format = "latex", booktabs = TRUE, longtable = TRUE, linesep = "",
      col.names = c("Future role", "Desirable", "Undesirable", "Mixed", "Public/central", "Commercial/general"),
      align = "lrrrrr") |>
  add_header_above(c(" " = 1, "Whole role sample" = 3, "Undesirable by outlet group" = 2)) |>
  kable_styling(latex_options = "repeat_header", font_size = 8) |>
  column_spec(1, width = "5.2cm") |> column_spec(2:4, width = "1.25cm") |>
  column_spec(5:6, width = "1.9cm")
```

*Note.* Whole-role denominators are 501, 312, 85, 439, and 162 articles, respectively. Outlet-specific denominators are the role counts in @tbl-role-prevalence. A role and evaluation must occur in the same attributed account. Different evaluations can coexist within an article; “Mixed” requires an explicitly mixed account. Missing and undecided evaluations remain in the denominators and are reported in Appendix A.

In Learning Partner, the tension concerned whether assistance developed or displaced understanding. A Dân trí report described a student’s experience of using ChatGPT at a university workshop:

> Drawing on his own experience, the student worried that overusing technology in learning might make students learn quickly but forget quickly, become superficial, and be less willing to think, reflect, or create.
>
> — Journalist’s account of a university student’s concern, *Dân trí* ([DTR24_022](https://dantri.com.vn/giao-duc/dung-chatgpt-lam-bai-sinh-vien-hoang-khi-kien-thuc-vao-nhanh-di-voi-20241113100850798.htm))

The report also described benefits and a lecturer’s recommendation to use ChatGPT as a supporting tool. Faster task completion and stronger learning were treated as different outcomes, making dependence a problem within the imagined learning relationship. Negative evaluations in this role were similarly frequent across the outlet groups: `r rp("FR_LEARNING_PARTNER", "DES_NEGATIVE", "public/central")`% in public/central and `r rp("FR_LEARNING_PARTNER", "DES_NEGATIVE", "commercial/general")`% in commercial/general articles containing it.

Educational Judgment showed a sharper outlet difference. Although the role’s overall prevalence was similar, negative evaluations appeared in `r rp("FR_EDUCATIONAL_JUDGMENT", "DES_NEGATIVE", "commercial/general")`% of commercial/general articles containing it, compared with `r rp("FR_EDUCATIONAL_JUDGMENT", "DES_NEGATIVE", "public/central")`% of public/central articles. Disagreement also concerned how credible assessment should be protected. A government-news report described technical detection and police–education coordination to prevent AI-enabled examination cheating ([BCP26_009](https://baochinhphu.vn/bo-cong-an-siet-chat-chong-gian-lan-bang-ai-tai-ky-thi-tot-nghiep-thpt-102260610082735862.htm)). A Tia Sáng commentary instead argued for assessment grounded in interaction with learners:

> Alternatives do exist. From mini oral defences to reflective portfolios, from supervised group assignments to staged reflective writing, all help restore human relationships in education and reduce dependence on machines. These are forms of assessment that do not exclude AI, but neither do they elevate it into a tool of moral surveillance.
>
> — Independent education researcher, authorial commentary, *Tia Sáng* ([TSG25_001](https://tiasang.com.vn/sinh-vien-viet-hay-bi-nghi-dung-ai-ai-co-quyen-phan-xet-4966355.html))

Both articles belonged to the public/central group. Their shared concern with credible achievement supported different practices: detection and enforcement in one account, dialogue and evidence of the learning process in the other. The latter offered a positively valued alternative while criticising detector-based judgments. Negative desirability therefore captures one part of critical discussion, rather than every proposal that questions an existing AI application.

Nor was National Development wholly affirmative. Its seven articles with linked negative evaluations all appeared in public/central outlets. In a VOV account, a university AI-capacity programme director warned that dependence could produce people able to operate technology without developing thought, weakening national capabilities ([VOV25_009](https://vov.vn/xa-hoi/ai-trong-giao-duc-va-bai-toan-dinh-hinh-the-he-cong-dan-so-post1237972.vov)). The same account promoted critical AI competence. National capability supplied a reason both to prepare people for AI and to challenge uses that might undermine that preparation.

Across the full sample, commercial/general articles contained negative evaluations more frequently (`r pct("desirability__DES_NEGATIVE", filter(main, outlet_group == "commercial/general"))`% versus `r pct("desirability__DES_NEGATIVE", filter(main, outlet_group == "public/central"))`%). Explicitly mixed accounts differed little between the groups (`r pct("desirability__DES_MIXED", filter(main, outlet_group == "commercial/general"))`% and `r pct("desirability__DES_MIXED", filter(main, outlet_group == "public/central"))`%). The existing primary-account designation provided a separate indication of emphasis: desirable evaluations occupied the primary position in `r pct("desirability__DES_POSITIVE", primary)`% of articles, compared with `r pct("desirability__DES_NEGATIVE", primary)`% for undesirable evaluations. Warnings were more widely included than selected as the principal evaluated future, while close reading showed that some critical interventions took the form of positively valued alternatives.

# Discussion

Vietnamese news gave unequal visibility to a shared set of educational AI futures. The strongest contrast lay between the broad presence of learning support, the institutional emphasis on preparation, and the concentration of negative evaluations around learning and assessment. Public/central coverage gave greater weight to AI Literacy and National Development; commercial/general coverage more often included negative assessments of Educational Judgment. This pattern explains how an affirmative direction can be sustained without eliminating disagreement over what AI should do in education.

The findings connect plurality to selection through public attention and institutional justification. National Development was not the most prevalent future overall, but it was substantially more frequent in public/central coverage and was articulated through public authorities, educational leadership, resources, and curricula. The draft-strategy account made this connection concrete by specifying a horizon for widespread AI use and the organisations expected to realise it. Taken together, these observations support an interpretation of preferential visibility for institutionally actionable futures: proposals gain a clearer route to implementation when they are connected to recognised authorities and concrete programmes. This is the communicative dimension of selection identified by the study. @bareis2022 locate the performative force of national AI imaginaries in policy commitments and resources; the present analysis shows how related directions are presented and justified in news.

Following the approach developed by @brause2024 and @brause2025, the analysis also shows why future roles need to be read through their other dimensions. Learning support, institutional efficiency, and national development are familiar expectations. Their significance becomes clearer when tied to particular relations and obligations. In one account, administrative relief enables teachers to concentrate on pupils. In another, technological change requires educational organisations to revise curricula and develop AI competence. Such connections give content to broad promises of improvement. They also make educational preparation appear necessary: once an AI-oriented future is treated as the setting in which people will live and work, education is called upon to equip them for it. This finding develops Rahm’s [-@rahm2023] account of education as a means of governing anticipated technological change.

The outlet comparison shows that institutional and commercial agendas can reinforce one another. National workforce formation was promoted through a commercial university’s competition as well as through government planning, while learning assistance was described by a technology-provider representative. These cases complement Nguyen et al.’s [-@nguyen2026] finding that developmental aspirations and industry participation coexist in Vietnamese AI reporting. The contribution here is to locate those connections within specific educational futures. The commercial/general group’s greater inclusion of negative evaluations does not amount to a uniformly oppositional position: its learning-support coverage was as extensive as public/central coverage, and the difference in negative assessment was much sharper for Educational Judgment than for Learning Partner.

Critical accounts qualified the direction of change in more than one way. The student’s concern separated efficient completion from retained understanding; the assessment commentary distinguished trustworthy judgment from reliance on detection. These are disagreements about what counts as educational improvement. They fit Rahm and Rahm-Skågeby’s [-@rahmskageby2023] argument that proposed technologies carry problem definitions, and Linderoth et al.’s [-@linderoth2024] finding that different visions of education can guide different responses to AI. Some responses restrict a practice, some redesign it, and others strengthen the capabilities needed to use AI. They need not form mutually exclusive futures.

The imbalance in desirability gives these disagreements their setting. Affirmative evaluations were far more widespread and more frequently primary, while negative evaluations clustered around learning and assessment. Yet the Tia Sáng account demonstrates why counting negative statements alone would understate the scope of criticism: a desired future based on dialogue can challenge technological control. The analytical distinction is therefore between evaluating an arrangement negatively and proposing a different arrangement, not between a positive mainstream and a single negative alternative. News makes both visible, although with unequal frequency and emphasis. For comparative education, this locates the contribution of media analysis between policy and practice: it reveals which educational expectations circulate with institutional justification and where the meaning of improvement remains open to dispute.

## Limitations

The corpus is bounded by Google News indexing and retrieval limits, selected domains and search vocabulary, title screening, and recoverable texts. Assessment and academic-integrity terms were explicitly included in queries and may have increased the visibility of Educational Judgment. Search vocabulary changed across periods, early years were sparse, and 2026 was incomplete. The analysis therefore describes the retrieved corpus rather than the distribution of all Vietnamese news. The approximate outlet groups capture publishing orientation and institutional affiliation, not a state–private ownership divide. Differences may also reflect outlet, year, event, and source composition.

AI-assisted extraction and coding are interpretive. Source-linked evidence and automated validation improve traceability but do not establish semantic validity or independent agreement. The five-role revision retained the other eleven fields and account boundaries, so errors in those earlier decisions could carry into the revised profiles. The researcher’s exploratory coding informed category development; it is not reported as a random reliability sample. Role breadth also affects prevalence: a broad learning relationship can encompass more proposals than a narrowly defined administrative function. Missing fields and unassigned roles remain in their stated denominators.

Article presence gives a brief mention and an extended discussion equal weight. Within-role profiles preserve linkage inside accounts but do not measure the strength of associations or imply that all listed features occur in a single proposition. Primary position is an existing coder judgment about the prominent arrangement, not a direct measure of headline placement, textual length, or editorial intention. Close readings illustrate differences in practice; those practices have not been separately coded as mutually exclusive categories. Desirability is target-specific and cannot serve as an exhaustive measure of criticism.

Repeated quotations and event material remain in the corpus as instances of circulation, so article counts do not represent independent endorsements. News evidence establishes neither audience acceptance nor implementation. The interpretation of selection concerns published visibility and justification; it cannot reconstruct editorial decisions, demonstrate government direction of particular stories, or establish which proposals received funding. Following these futures into institutional decisions and educational practice would require additional evidence.

# Conclusion

Five familiar futures organised Vietnamese educational AI coverage, but they received unequal attention. Learning Partner and AI Literacy were the most prevalent; Educational Judgment carried substantial debate, while Educational Management and National Development occupied smaller shares. Their profiles showed how educational goals were connected to different speakers, reasons, and responsibilities. Public/central outlets gave greater weight to preparation and collective development, while commercial/general outlets more frequently included negative evaluations of educational judgment. The groups shared much of the same repertoire, with differences in what they emphasised and how it was evaluated.

The central finding is that plurality coexists with an affirmative direction of change. Institutional programmes make AI-related preparation and development publicly actionable, while critical accounts question whether particular uses support learning and credible judgment. Some of those accounts advocate positively valued alternatives, so their contribution cannot be reduced to negative sentiment. News analysis reveals which futures receive wider visibility and institutional justification, and which educational questions remain contested within that direction.

# Appendix B. Sensitivity of selected outlet comparisons

These checks retain the main sample and existing coding. Primary-only comparison counts the account already designated primary in each article. Single-outlet omission repeats the full article-presence comparison after removing each outlet in turn. The table reports public/central minus commercial/general percentage-point differences; omission ranges are descriptive ranges, not confidence intervals.

```{r}
#| label: setup-sensitivity
#| include: false
selected_codes <- c("future_role__FR_NATIONAL_DEVELOPMENT",
  "technology_object__OBJ_GENERATIVE", "desirability__DES_NEGATIVE",
  "action__ACT_RULES", "action__ACT_EVALUATE")
gap <- function(data, code) {
  a <- filter(data, outlet_group == "public/central")
  b <- filter(data, outlet_group == "commercial/general")
  100 * (article_count(code, a) / nrow(a) - article_count(code, b) / nrow(b))
}
sensitivity <- map_dfr(selected_codes, function(code) {
  omitted <- vapply(unique(main$outlet_domain), function(domain)
    gap(filter(main, outlet_domain != domain), code), numeric(1))
  tibble(code, full = gap(main, code), primary = gap(primary, code),
         low = min(omitted), high = max(omitted))
}) |> left_join(labels |> transmute(code = paste0(field, "__", code), category), by = "code")
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-sensitivity
#| tbl-cap: "Selected outlet differences under primary-only aggregation and outlet omission (percentage points)."
sensitivity |>
  transmute(Category = category, Full = sprintf("%+.1f", full),
    Primary = sprintf("%+.1f", primary), Omission = sprintf("%+.1f to %+.1f", low, high)) |>
  kbl(format = "latex", booktabs = TRUE, longtable = TRUE, linesep = "",
      col.names = c("Category", "All accounts", "Primary only", "Omit one outlet")) |>
  kable_styling(latex_options = "repeat_header", font_size = 9) |>
  column_spec(1, width = "6.2cm")
```

Negative evaluations appeared in `r pct("desirability__DES_NEGATIVE", filter(primary, outlet_group == "public/central"))`% of public/central and `r pct("desirability__DES_NEGATIVE", filter(primary, outlet_group == "commercial/general"))`% of commercial/general articles when only primary accounts were counted. The group difference was therefore smaller than for presence anywhere in an article. This distinction separates the inclusion of a negative account from its designation as the principal future arrangement; positively evaluated critical alternatives can still occupy that primary position.
